title: Ramadan: the last ten
hook: the Prophet ﷺ tightened his belt and woke his family in the last ten (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mosque in Ramadan: a night prayer kept voluntary out of mercy, and a table where whoever walks in gets fed. Your line: the community table. Did you find an iftar, or share a meal with someone? Today, the end of the month, when things speed up. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-one.

In everyday English, tightening your belt means cutting back. Spending less. Getting by. In a report from 'A'ishah in Sahih al-Bukhari, it means almost the opposite. She describes what the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, did when the last ten nights of Ramadan began. In paraphrase: he tightened his waist-wrapper, he brought his nights to life, and he woke his family. Not cutting back. Gearing up. The month was nearly over, and instead of coasting toward the finish, he went harder. Today: the last ten.
screen: `TIGHTENING YOUR BELT: CUTTING BACK?` → `HE TIGHTENED HIS WAIST-WRAPPER.` → `GEARING UP, NOT COASTING.`

segments.voice: Take her three phrases one at a time. He tightened his waist-wrapper. Scholars read this in two ways. Some say it means rolling up your sleeves, serious effort, the way a worker cinches a belt before lifting. Others say it means he withdrew from his wives for those nights to give himself to worship. Some hold both. He brought his nights to life: he stayed awake in prayer instead of sleeping through them. And he woke his family. He didn't keep the nights to himself. He went to the people he lived with and got them up too. Second, why these nights. The Qur'an names a night: the Night of Power. Surah al-Qadr says, in Pickthall's words: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." And in another report in al-Bukhari, the Prophet tells people to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten. The report names no single night. So the way to find it is to show up for all of them. Third, some go further and stay in the mosque. 'A'ishah says in al-Bukhari that he kept i'tikaf, a retreat in the mosque, in the last ten, and his wives kept it after him. Fourth, what to say if you find the night. In al-Tirmidhi, 'A'ishah asks him exactly that. He teaches her a short prayer asking Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon. Not for wealth. Not for a sign. For pardon. So the last ten have a shape: effort, wakefulness, family, retreat, and at the center, one plain request.
screen: `THREE THINGS 'A'ISHAH SAW.` · `THE NIGHT OF POWER, UNNAMED.` · `I'TIKAF: A RETREAT IN THE MOSQUE.` · `AT THE CENTER, ASKING PARDON.`

segments.voice: The practice: wake for one night. Not tonight necessarily. Settle, and breathe, and choose a night, in Ramadan if you keep it, or any night this week if you don't. Picture the alarm going off in the dark. The house quiet. You sit up instead of rolling over. What would you do with that hour? Pray, read, sit in silence, write down what you're sorry for and what you're thankful for. Hold that picture for the rest of the bell. If you pray, you can ask for pardon, the way the Prophet taught 'A'ishah. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, which ends in ten nights of extra effort, with the Night of Power hidden somewhere among them. Today's word.
Your line: tighten the belt. Today, set the alarm for the night you chose, and decide what the first five minutes will be. Tomorrow, Eid al-Fitr: the day. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, Muslims add night prayer and look for the Night of Power in the odd nights, as hadiths in al-Bukhari describe; some stay in the mosque in a retreat called i'tikaf, and some repeat the short prayer for pardon the Prophet taught 'A'ishah, kept in al-Tirmidhi.

trapdoor: what you thought: the end of Ramadan is when things wind down.
what it means: the last ten nights are when the Prophet went hardest: awake, waking his family, looking for the Night of Power.
what a scholar hears: 'A'ishah's three phrases in al-Bukhari, the two readings of the tightened waist-wrapper, and the odd nights of the last ten.
